title: What identity, session and authorization model fits a public product on Cloudflare, testable locally?
summary: Start from the existing design record at /notes/auth/ (GitHub OAuth, HMAC cookie, D1 schema) and challenge it for a public audience: providers, passkeys, magic links, hosted auth vs DIY on Workers, sessions, topic-scoped roles, anonymous-with-level identity, multiple profiles, local user switching.

title: Server/plugins/Auth.js is dev-only Node session auth, not a Cloudflare pattern
summary: Server/plugins/Auth.js wires express-session plus session-file-store, google-auth-library (Google One Tap ID-token verify), cookie and cookie-parser into the Node dev server; sessions live server-side in a file store keyed by a signed cookie, and it also authenticates websockets by reading that cookie. It runs only under node server.js (Server/ is dev-only per CLAUDE.md), has four npm dependencies, and its file-store session model has no Workers equivalent (no filesystem at the edge) - none of its code or shape transfers to a Workers/D1 design.

title: Apple 4.8: any third-party/social login on iOS needs a privacy-limited equivalent, not necessarily Apple itself
summary: developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/ 4.8 Login Services (fetched 2026-09-04): apps using a third-party/social login (Facebook, Google, GitHub, etc.) to set up the primary account must also offer an equivalent that limits data to name+email, lets the user hide their email, and does not collect ad-tracking interactions without consent. Exempt only if the app exclusively uses its own account system - so GitHub-OAuth-only still triggers the rule on iOS; a second option (Apple, or an email/password/magic-link that meets those three criteria) is required, not necessarily Sign in with Apple by name.

title: Passkey ecosystem readiness is near-saturated on major platforms; first-try enrollment is not
summary: Corbado Passkey Benchmark 2026 (corbado.com/passkey-benchmark-2026, fetched 2026-09-04): platform readiness (WebAuthn client capability) reaches about 99% iOS web, 97% Android, 91% macOS by end of 2025. But first-try web passkey ENROLLMENT success is far lower and uneven: 49-83% iOS, 41-67% Android, 41-65% macOS, only 25-39% Windows. Windows is the weak link - a passkey-first MVP should expect roughly 2 in 3 Windows users to fail enrollment on the first try.

title: Workers implement the standard WebCrypto API, enabling dependency-free WebAuthn signature verification
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/web-crypto/ (fetched 2026-09-04): Workers implement the full WebCrypto standard (crypto.subtle), the same API used to verify a WebAuthn assertion signature. Verifying a passkey login therefore needs zero npm dependencies - only building/parsing the CBOR attestation and authenticatorData by hand, which existing MIT-licensed reference code (e.g. AprilNEA/webauthn-workers on GitHub) already does for Workers.

title: SMS OTP fraud-share stats (pumping/toll fraud) come only from fraud-vendor blogs, not neutral measurement
summary: Search results on SMS pumping/toll fraud (engagelab.com, prelude.so, telnyx.com, fetched 2026-09-04) cite figures like 11.83% of 205M requests fraudulent, unprotected systems at 5-15% fraud share, and AIT costing brands 1.16B dollars in 2023. Every source is a vendor selling OTP fraud protection, so the numbers are directionally real (toll fraud is a documented telecom problem) but not independently audited - treat as the size of the problem, not a precise rate for this platform.

title: Clerk: free to 50,000 monthly retained users, then 0.02 dollars per MRU up to 100k
summary: clerk.com/pricing (fetched 2026-09-04): Hobby plan is free up to 50,000 MRU (monthly RETAINED users - counts only users who return 24h+ after signup, a stricter/smaller metric than raw MAU). Pro is 25 dollars/month (20 annual) and includes the same 50k, then 0.02 dollars/MRU for 50,001-100,000, stepping down at higher volume. At 1k and 10k MAU: free. At 100k MAU: about 25 + 50,000*0.02 = 1,025 dollars/month, likely less once translated from MAU to the stricter MRU metric.

title: Auth0 pricing tiers are internally inconsistent across the vendors own marketing surfaces
summary: auth0.com/pricing (fetched 2026-09-04) states Free covers up to 25,000 MAU with social login and passwordless. But the same page prices paid B2C Essentials at 35 dollars/month for only 500 MAU included, 0.07 dollars/MAU overage after (about 700 dollars/month at 10k MAU), and B2C Professional at 240 dollars/month also for 500 MAU with no published overage rate, auto-upgrading tiers after 3 months over. A team needing MFA, RBAC or custom DB connections falls out of the 25k free tier at far lower volume than the topline number implies - the free-tier MAU number and the paid-tier MAU number describe different feature sets, not the same product.

title: Supabase Auth: free to 50,000 MAU, Pro (25 dollars/month) covers 100,000 MAU
summary: supabase.com/pricing (fetched 2026-09-04): Free plan includes 50,000 MAU. Pro plan is 25 dollars/month base and includes 100,000 MAU, then 0.00325 dollars per additional MAU (500,000 MAU would run about 1,300 dollars/month). At 1k, 10k, and 100k MAU the cost is the same 25 dollars/month Pro base fee - the cheapest of the three hosted options compared at 10k MAU, and it ships with a real Postgres database alongside auth rather than only an identity product.

title: WorkOS and Stytch consumer pricing looks free but is not sized for open public signup
summary: Secondary aggregators (guptadeepak.com/ciam-compass, workos.com/blog, fetched 2026-09-04) report WorkOS AuthKit free to 1,000,000 MAU but built B2B-first, lacking B2C features like progressive profiling and adaptive MFA - vendors recommend Auth0/Stytch/Descope for consumer apps instead. Stytch is reported free to 10,000 MAU then priced per SSO/SCIM connection (125 dollars/connection), an enterprise-integration metric that does not map cleanly onto a public consumer product. Neither was verified against its own pricing page directly in this pass - flagged for the skeptic check.

title: Cloudflare Access bills 7 dollars per authenticated user/month past 50 free - a gate, not a signup system
summary: Sources on Cloudflare Zero Trust pricing (fetched 2026-09-04, cross-referenced against the known Cloudflare Access product shape) report free to 50 users then 7 dollars/user/month pay-as-you-go with no cap, where a seat is one authenticated login event via an identity provider. At 10,000 public users that is roughly 70,000 dollars/month, and Access has no self-service registration, profile storage, or app-owned user table - it gates an app behind an allowed identity list, which is the opposite shape from open public signup.

title: Cloudflare Access is a no for this product: priced and shaped for gating known users, not public registration
summary: Access authenticates a bounded list of identities behind an IdP login (employees, contractors) and charges per authenticated seat with no free public tier at scale - the brief wants open signup for anyone, with profiles, roles and D1-backed app data the product owns. Access cannot hold a users/profiles schema, does not offer email/social/passkey signup flows to the general public, and its cost model (per-seat, no volume discount curve published) is built for internal tooling. It stays useful for gating the admin/staff surface of this same product, which is a different, smaller audience than the public one this brief is about.

title: better-auth ships a native Cloudflare D1 adapter, but it is still a real npm dependency
summary: npmjs.com/package/better-auth-cloudflare and github.com/better-auth/better-auth (fetched 2026-09-04): Better Auth now accepts a D1 binding directly with no ORM required, handling query execution and batch writes through D1 native API (D1 has no interactive transactions, so it uses batch() for atomicity). This is the most Workers-native of the auth libraries surveyed, but it is still a package to vendor, update and audit - it breaks the /notes/auth/ zero-dependency-in-production stance, which a hand-rolled OAuth-code-flow-plus-WebCrypto approach does not.

title: Build vs buy for the MVP: DIY on Workers, extending the existing /notes/auth/ design, not a hosted vendor
summary: At MVP scale (well under 10k MAU) every hosted option (Clerk, Supabase Auth) is cheap or free, so price is not the deciding factor - control and static-site fit are. The existing /notes/auth/ record already proves GitHub OAuth plus a WebCrypto-HMAC cookie needs zero dependencies and keeps worker/ as the only new runtime surface; adding a hosted vendor means a new domain in the auth flow, a webhook/sync problem to keep D1 profiles in sync with the vendor's user store, and a migration cost if the vendor is dropped later. Revisit Supabase Auth (cheapest, ships Postgres too) only if session/role logic outgrows what one Worker file can hold.

title: Cloudflare raised the request/response header limit from 32KB to 128KB in October 2025
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2025-10-16-header-limit-increase (fetched 2026-09-04): as of 2025-10-16 Cloudflare CDN and Workers accept up to 128KB total for request/response headers, up from a prior 32KB total / 16KB per-header limit. Headroom exists for large cookies, but the browsers own per-cookie cap (see RFC 6265 entry) is the tighter real constraint on a single signed session cookie, not Cloudflares edge.

title: RFC 6265 sets the practical cookie ceiling at 4096 bytes per cookie
summary: rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265 (fetched 2026-09-04): general-use user agents SHOULD support at least 4096 bytes per cookie, counting name+value+attributes together, and most browsers hold to this despite it being a SHOULD not a MUST. A signed HMAC-SHA256 session payload (user_id, expiry, token_epoch, base64) plus attributes comfortably fits in a few hundred bytes, so this is not a binding constraint for the stateless-cookie design - it would only bite a design that tried to pack role lists or profile data into the cookie itself.

title: D1 free tier: 5M rows read and 100K rows written per day; paid is 0.001 dollars per million reads
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/pricing (via search, fetched 2026-09-04): free tier gives 5,000,000 rows read/day and 100,000 rows written/day, resetting daily at 00:00 UTC; paid tier is 0.001 dollars per million rows read and 1.00 dollars per million rows written, with the Workers Paid plan (5 dollars/month) including 25 billion reads and 50 million writes. A session-table read on every authenticated request is one indexed row read - at even 1M authenticated requests/day this is inside the free tier and, past it, costs about 1 dollar per billion requests. Cost is not what makes table-backed sessions expensive; latency and schema upkeep are.

title: D1 read replication plus the Sessions API cuts cross-region read latency by over 90 percent
summary: blog.cloudflare.com/d1-read-replication-beta and a practitioner report (jackpearce.co.uk, fetched 2026-09-04): D1 read replicas place read-only SQLite copies near clients globally; without the Sessions API all reads still hit the single primary. One measured case: cumulative D1 read latency for Australian users dropped from 1,800ms to 78ms (about 96 percent) after enabling replication with the Sessions API, which also guarantees sequential consistency so a user does not see stale reads of their own writes. This undercuts the /notes/auth/ verdicts assumption that a D1 session lookup costs a slow global round trip on every request - it did, before this beta; it need not now.

title: run_worker_first can be scoped to a path list, keeping the API first-party without taxing static assets
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/routing/worker-script (via search, fetched 2026-09-04): default run_worker_first=false serves matching static files with no Worker invocation (no billing); setting it true runs the Worker unconditionally, but it also accepts a list of patterns, e.g. run_worker_first: [/api/*], so only API routes pay for a Worker invocation while every asset request stays free static serving. This is exactly the shape /notes/auth/ wants - api and assets on one origin, so the session cookie is first-party with no CORS or cross-site cookie problem.

title: SameSite=Lax alone does not stop CSRF; check Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site on mutating requests too
summary: OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet (cheatsheetseries.owasp.org, fetched 2026-09-04): SameSite cookies are defense in depth, not a complete CSRF defense - Lax still allows some cross-site GET navigations to carry the cookie, so an app that mutates state on GET remains exposed. Recommended layering: keep mutations on POST/PUT/DELETE only, check Sec-Fetch-Site first where the browser sends it, fall back to Origin (or Referer) header validation, and keep SameSite=Lax as the second layer. This confirms /notes/auth/'s also check Origin on every mutating request line as correct, not optional.

title: A Durable Object has an official soft limit of 1,000 requests per second
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/limits (fetched 2026-09-04): a single Durable Object instance has a soft request-rate limit of 1,000 req/s, SQLite-backed storage up to 10GB per object, and up to 5 minutes of active CPU time per request when configured. A DO-per-user session/rate-limit object (one object named by user id) stays far under this limit for any one user, but a DO-per-topic design for a busy topic could approach it under real concurrent load - shard across multiple objects if so.

title: Workers KV eventual consistency has a documented worst case of 60 seconds globally
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/kv/concepts/how-kv-works (fetched 2026-09-04): a KV write is usually visible immediately at the colo that made it, but other global locations may take up to 60 seconds (or a little more) to see the change, driven by a cache TTL that defaults to and cannot go below 60 seconds. A KV-backed ban/revocation list is fast and nearly free to read but is not instant everywhere - a banned user can keep a live session for up to about a minute in the worst case, which needs to be an explicit, accepted number if bans are a hard requirement.

title: Sessions for the MVP: keep the stateless HMAC cookie, add a KV ban-check on every request
summary: The /notes/auth/ design (stateless cookie plus token_epoch, re-signed on use) still fits day-to-day auth - zero I/O to verify. What it cannot do is ban instantly, which this public brief needs unlike the internal dev site. Fix: one KV.get(banned:user_id) check per authenticated request - near-free, no schema, worst case about 60s propagation (see the KV consistency finding), which beats a 30-day-or-refresh delay by orders of magnitude and matches CDN-purge-grade expectations elsewhere on the web. Reserve a real D1 sessions table (now cheap, and fast with read replication) for the day per-device revoke or a full audit trail becomes a real requirement, not before.

title: 60-second KV ban propagation may not be enough against a fast coordinated raid
summary: A single troll banned a minute late is a non-event. A coordinated raid - many accounts posting in the same window, bans issued in a burst - could see new posts land inside that 60-second window before every edge colo has the updated ban list; the failure mode is a burst outrunning propagation, not one slow ban. No source found measures this for a moderation use case specifically - it is plausible, not demonstrated. Falsifiable by load-testing a simulated raid against a real KV-backed ban check before shipping.

title: Authorization: one can(user, action, topic) function in the Worker; two role scopes, not more
summary: Standard RBAC practice (no single vendor doc needed - this is the shape every one of the surveyed hosted providers converges on) splits policy into global roles (owner, admin, staff - platform-wide power) and resource-scoped roles (topic owner, moderator, member, guest - power inside one topic). Put every check behind one function the Worker calls before a mutation; the client only hides UI for a denied action, it never trusts itself. Do not add a third scope (e.g. per-channel roles) until a topic actually has channels that need to diverge from the topic-level role - the brief already flags reputation/level gates as the community topic owning that, not this layer.

title: Cloudflare Turnstile is free with no request cap on the Standard plan
summary: Search results on Turnstile pricing (fetched 2026-09-04, cross-referenced with Cloudflare's own Turnstile product page shape) report the Standard plan is free with no per-verification cost or volume cap; scaling into per-endpoint bot policies and custom risk thresholds requires Enterprise Bot Management starting around 2,000 dollars/month. For rate-limiting anonymous participation (the browser challenge, not the volume-based product), the free tier is the whole answer - no cost trade-off to make at MVP scale.

title: Anonymous plus topic plus level is a quasi-identifier combination, same shape as k-anonymity re-identification
summary: K-anonymity research (Sweeney's foundational paper, epic.org/wp-content/uploads/privacy/reidentification/Sweeney_Article.pdf, fetched 2026-09-04) shows a small combination of non-identifying attributes can single out a person when cross-referenced with outside knowledge - classically zip+birthdate+sex. Anonymous - Level 5 JavaScript is the same shape: in a small topic, level plus activity timing plus topic could narrow to one person, especially if someone already suspects who it is offline. This is a general principle applied to this design, not a study of it - a real risk to design against (cap level display granularity in small topics), not a proven leak.

title: Anonymous identity: session-scoped by default, signed device id, upgrade path preserves progress
summary: Sign a random anon id into a cookie/localStorage value (same HMAC helper the real session already needs), scoped to the browser, not permanent by design - a cleared browser is a fresh anonymous identity, which is an acceptable and honest trade-off, not a bug. Gate posting/voting behind Turnstile (free) plus per-ip and per-anon-id rate limits at the Worker. Upgrading to a real account should re-key existing anon-id-owned rows to the new user_id in one transaction so level/history is not lost - this needs anon contributions to be owned by the anon id from day one, which is a schema decision worth making before the first anonymous write ships.

title: Multiple profiles: split profile_id from user_id in schema now, ship exactly one profile per user at MVP
summary: Every query keyed by profile_id instead of user_id is a real, permanent cost - every join, every RLS-equivalent check, every URL gains a dimension - so decide the column shape once, at the start. Cost of deciding now is near zero (an extra join on a table with one row per user); cost of retrofitting it later touches every table. Recommend: add profiles(id, user_id, ...) as its own table from day one, but do not build a profile-switcher UI or allow more than one row per user_id until a creator/brand need is proven - see the Google Brand Account finding for the shape to copy when that day comes.

title: Google Brand Account: one login, multiple manageable identities, no separate password
summary: support.google.com/accounts/answer/7001996 (fetched 2026-09-04): a YouTube/Google Brand Account is a distinct identity from a personal account, but it is not a separate credential - one or more people manage it through their own existing Google logins, with owner/manager roles controlling who can act as it. This is the precedent worth copying if this platform ever needs creator/brand profiles: profile_id distinct from user_id, multiple user_ids granted access to one profile_id, no second password ever created.

title: wrangler d1 has first-class local migrate and seed commands, data persists across dev runs
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/d1/best-practices/local-development (fetched 2026-09-04): wrangler d1 migrations apply DB_NAME --local applies schema locally, wrangler d1 execute DB --local --file=./seeds/dev.sql loads seed data, both against a local SQLite file wrangler manages - the Worker code uses the same env.DB binding as production. Since Wrangler v3, local data persists across wrangler dev restarts by default, so a reset needs an explicit DROP TABLE at the top of a reseed script rather than relying on a clean start.

title: Local dev recipe: wrangler dev plus seeded D1, a dev-only session-forcing header, Playwright contexts
summary: wrangler.jsonc gets a d1_databases binding; migrations/0001_init.sql plus seeds/dev.sql seed 3-5 fake users (one per role) via wrangler d1 execute --local; a dev-only Worker branch, guarded by an env flag never set in production, accepts ?as=<handle> and mints a signed cookie for that user with no OAuth round trip, so switching identity is one URL change - real GitHub OAuth against a localhost callback still works for end-to-end checks. For multi-user interaction, one browser.newContext() per fake user in Playwright (separate cookie jars) against one wrangler dev instance covers concurrent multi-tab testing and the anonymous path (a context with no cookie) without multiple real browsers.

title: GDPR/CCPA data minimization: collect and keep only what is necessary for the stated purpose
summary: CCPA section 1798.100(c) and GDPR purpose-limitation principle (via trustarc.com/resource/data-minimization-gdpr-ccpa-privacy-laws, fetched 2026-09-04): collection, use, retention and sharing of personal information must be reasonably necessary and proportionate to the disclosed purpose; data must not be kept past the point it is needed, and unnecessary fields are pure liability with no offsetting value if breached. Applied to a users table: no field should exist that the product does not actively use today - phone number, birthdate and IP history are the likely candidates to exclude or short-retain unless a specific feature (SMS auth, COPPA gating, abuse investigation) needs them.

title: COPPA: no age gate is required for a general-audience site, but actual knowledge of a under-13 user changes that
summary: ftc.gov COPPA FAQ and Federal Register 2024 final rule text (fetched 2026-09-04): operators of general-audience sites need not ask a users age, and are not liable for under-13 users they have no actual knowledge of. But if an operator screens age in a neutral way (e.g. a birthdate field) and a user enters one showing under 13, that knowledge cannot be discarded - the operator must then either get verifiable parental consent or serve that user an experience that collects no personal information. Practical implication: either do not ask for birthdate at signup, or be ready to branch the flow the moment one comes back under 13.

title: R2 avatar storage: free 10GB and 1M writes/month, then 0.015 dollars per GB-month, zero egress fee
summary: developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing (via search, fetched 2026-09-04): free tier includes 10 GB-month storage, 1,000,000 Class A (write/list) operations and 10,000,000 Class B (read) operations monthly; paid Standard storage is 0.015 dollars/GB-month, Class A ops 4.50 dollars/million, Class B ops 0.36 dollars/million, with no egress charge at all (R2's main differentiator from S3). Avatars (small images, read-heavy, write-rare) are a close-to-free R2 workload at MVP scale - the free tier alone likely covers tens of thousands of users worth of avatar storage and serving.

title: Transactional email (magic links) needs only a fetch POST on Workers, no vendor SDK
summary: resend.com/docs/send-with-cloudflare-workers and developers.cloudflare.com/workers/tutorials/send-emails-with-postmark (fetched 2026-09-04): both Resend and Postmark send email over a plain HTTPS POST with a bearer/server token header - Postmarks own JS library is not supported on Workers at all, and a Resend user reports replacing the SDK with seven lines of fetch. A magic-link flow (mint a signed token, POST the email via fetch, verify the token on click) needs zero new dependencies, consistent with the zero-dependency stance in /notes/auth/.

title: Profiles/settings: small D1 row plus R2 avatar, public-by-default limited to handle, avatar, topic levels
summary: profiles(user_id, handle, avatar_r2_key, bio, created_at) in D1, the avatar file itself in R2 under a key derived from user_id (not guessable sequential ids). Public by default: handle, avatar, badges/levels earned, join date - the same shape a GitHub profile already exposes, so it sets no new expectation. Private by default: email, provider/provider_id, IP history, any birthdate collected - these never render to another user and are excluded from any public profile API response by construction (a separate query/serializer, not a field-level flag that can be forgotten).

title: Legal minimum for the MVP users table: no phone, no birthdate, no raw IP retained past abuse window
summary: Given data minimization (GDPR/CCPA) and COPPA actual-knowledge risk, the leanest defensible users table for MVP: id, provider, provider_id, handle, avatar_url, token_epoch, created_at (already the /notes/auth/ shape) plus email only if a provider or magic-link needs it to function. Do not collect birthdate unless a feature requires an age gate - collecting it creates COPPA branching obligations for no benefit today. Log IP per request for abuse/rate-limiting but do not join it to the permanent profile, and set a short retention window on any raw request-log table holding it. GDPR/CCPA export and delete then become one query per table keyed on user_id.

title: Providers for the MVP: GitHub plus Google, magic link as fallback, defer Apple, passkeys, phone
summary: GitHub (existing verdict, right audience) plus Google (broadest reach, same OAuth-code-flow-plus-WebCrypto shape, no new machinery) as the two social options; email magic link as the no-account fallback. This triggers Apple 4.8 on iOS (two social logins offered) - magic link itself likely satisfies the required equivalent (name/email only, hideable, no ad tracking), so a literal Apple button may not be required; verify with a real iOS submission before trusting this reading. Defer: Apple as its own button, passkeys (real WebAuthn work, and Windows first-try enrollment is weak per Corbado), phone/SMS (fraud-vendor data shows real toll-fraud cost, no offsetting benefit here).

title: Does a magic-link-only second option actually satisfy Apple 4.8, or does App Review expect Apple by name in practice
summary: The guideline text (fetched from developer.apple.com, see the 4.8 finding) does not require Sign in with Apple specifically, only an equivalent meeting three privacy criteria - and magic link plausibly meets them. But App Review is a human process with reviewer discretion, and forum threads (developer.apple.com/forums) show real rejections even when apps believed they complied. Not resolvable by reading the policy alone - closes only with an actual TestFlight/App Review submission, or a direct answer from Apple Developer Relations.

title: Is a 60-second KV ban-propagation window fast enough for this platforms actual abuse profile
summary: No source measured moderation-specific ban propagation under real raid conditions (see the KV theory entry) - this is a judgment call about acceptable risk for a specific community, not a technical fact research can settle. Closes only once the platform has real moderation incidents to look back on, or a deliberate simulated-raid load test is run against the design before launch.

title: Do WorkOS and Stytch actually fit a public consumer product, or only their own marketing pages say so
summary: Entry on WorkOS/Stytch pricing here was built from aggregator and vendor-blog sources, not each vendors own pricing page fetched directly - flagged in the skeptic pass. Both vendors public pricing pages (workos.com/pricing, stytch.com/pricing) should be fetched directly before this platform seriously evaluates either, since the aggregator numbers conflict with each other on Stytch's exact free-tier shape.

title: Skeptic check: Auth0 free-tier MAU figure disagrees across sources, 7500 vs 25000
summary: An early aggregator hit (auth0pricing.com, via search) claimed free to 7,500 MAU, then paid tiers; two direct fetches of auth0.com/pricing itself both said free to 25,000 MAU (fetched 2026-09-04). Trusting the primary page over the aggregator, but flagging the disagreement per the research discipline - a stale aggregator page or a since-changed Auth0 plan could explain it, and this should be re-verified at the moment any real Auth0 decision is made, not assumed current.

title: Skeptic counter to the deanonymization theory: real platforms accept the residual risk and coarsen display, they do not remove levels
summary: Stack Overflow, Reddit and Discord all show pseudonymous reputation/activity next to a persistent handle, accepting the same quasi-identifier risk the theory entry describes - the mainstream answer is not don't show a level next to anonymous, it is round the number, do not timestamp it precisely, and do not combine it with other free-text fields (bio, post history) that narrow the combination further. Full removal of level display would defeat the point of the anonymous-with-reputation feature the brief asks for.
